extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Euclidean plane geometry (undergraduate/advanced-secondary)
extracted.subtask_description: A sequence of classical Euclidean propositions (theorems, problems, corollaries, and exercises) concerning circles, chords, tangents, angles, and constructions; intended as statements and proofs to learn and apply circle geometry results.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. VIII — Theorem (lines from a point outside a circle)
rubrics_metrics.description: If from any point (P) outside a circle, lines (PA, PB, PC, &c.) be drawn to the concave circumference, then—1. The maximum is that which passes through the centre. 2. Of the others, that which is nearer to the one through the centre is greater than the one more remote. Again, if lines be drawn to the convex circumference—3. The minimum is that whose production passes through the centre. 4. Of the others, that which is nearer to the minimum is less than one more remote. 5. From the given point (P) there can be drawn two equal lines to the concave or the convex circumference, both of which make equal angles with the line passing through the centre. 6. More than two equal lines cannot be drawn from the given point (P) to either circumference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full demonstration is given: compare sums of sides, triangle comparisons, and limiting arguments; includes constructions (joining centre O to points) and corollaries: (1) If PI be produced to meet the circle again in L, PL = PB. (2) If two equal lines be drawn from P to either circumference the diameter through P bisects the angle between them and the intercepted parts are equal. (3) If P is common centre of circles with radii drawn to circumference of HDE, then minimal radius circle has contact of first kind, maximal has contact of second kind, and intermediate radii give intersections in two points. Exercises follow for related locus and extremal problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. IX — Theorem (more than two equal lines imply centre)
rubrics_metrics.description: A point (P) within a circle (ABC), from which more than two equal lines (PA, PB, PC, &c.) can be drawn to the circumference, is the centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: if P not centre, only two equal lines possible [ref. VII]; or by intersection of angle bisectors—bisectors of equal chords pass through centre; intersection of bisectors is centre. Corollary: the unique centre characterization used in subsequent propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. X — Theorem (coincident circles if >2 intersections)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two circles have more than two points common, they must coincide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: pick three common points A,B,C and show centres coincide (equal radii from one centre to three points -> centre equals centre of other circle). Corollary: Two non-coinciding circles cannot have more than two common points. Compare with axiom that two straight lines not coinciding cannot have more than one point common.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XI — Theorem (internal contact centres collinear)
rubrics_metrics.description: If one circle (CPD) touches another circle (APB) internally at any point P, the line joining the centres must pass through that point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: assume centre of smaller circle not on line OP; compare distances to show impossibility. Alternative proof: consider circle with centre at E and radius EP cuts APB at P but touches—impossible. Corollaries and observation: point of contact counts as two intersections; the result is a limiting case of intersecting circles bisector property. Exercises illustrate related constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XII — Theorem (external contact centres collinear)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two circles (PCF, PDE) have external contact at any point P, the line joining their centres must pass through that point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: suppose centres not collinear with P, derive triangle inequality contradiction by summing radii and chord lengths; or use limiting/contradiction argument with a circle centred at B with radius BP cutting but touching PCF in P—impossible. Observation: XI and XII combined: 'If two circles touch each other at any point, the centres and that point are collinear.' Corollaries: point of contact counts as two intersections; touching circles cannot have any other common point.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XIII — Theorem (no double contact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two circles cannot have double contact, that is, cannot touch each other in two points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: if two contacts A and B existed, centres would be collinear with both A,B, so AB would be diameter of each ⇒ same centre ⇒ circles coincide, contradiction. Alternative argument: perpendicular bisector must pass through both centres—impossible. Also follows from fact that a contact counts as two intersections and two contacts would equal four intersections (impossible). Exercises apply previous corollaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XIV — Theorem (equal chords equally distant from centre)
rubrics_metrics.description: In equal circles—1. equal chords (AB, CD) are equally distant from the centre. 2. chords which are equally distant from the centre are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses perpendicular from centre bisecting chord and Pythagorean relations: equal chord halves and equal radii give equality of distances. Exercise: locus problems—e.g., locus of midpoint of a sliding chord is a circle; locus of a fixed point on chord is a circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XV — Theorem (diameter is greatest chord; nearer → greater)
rubrics_metrics.description: The diameter (AB) is the greatest chord in a circle; and of the others, the chord (CD) which is nearer to the centre is greater than (EF) one more remote, and the greater is nearer to the centre than the less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via comparing sums and right-triangle relations (OG, OH perpendiculars). Exercises: shortest chord through given point is perpendicular to diameter through that point; construction problems to draw chords of given length through given points; extremal problems for chords and inscribed figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XVI — Theorem (perpendicular at extremity is tangent)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1. The perpendicular (BI) to the diameter (AB) of a circle at its extremity (B) touches the circle at that point. 2. Any other line (BH) through the same point cuts the circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: show any other point on BI is outside circle hence BI meets circle only at B (tangent). Alternative proofs: tangent perpendicular to radius at point of contact via limiting secant argument. Exercises include properties of tangents between concentric circles and constructing tangents parallel/perpendicular to given lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XVII — Problem (construct tangent from external point)
rubrics_metrics.description: From a given point (P) without a given circle (BCD) to draw a tangent to the circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: join OP (O centre), with O as centre and OP as radius describe circle APE; erect CA at right angles to OP, join OA intersecting circle BCD in B; BP is the tangent. Demonstration uses congruent triangles AOC and POB; corollary: two tangents from P are equal. Exercises: various tangent-related problems including radical axis, radical centre, equal tangents to three circles, geometric relations OF·OP = radius^2, inverse points, and drawing common tangents.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XVIII — Theorem (radius to tangent perpendicular)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a line (CD) touch a circle, the line (OC) from the centre to the point of contact is perpendicular to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: assume OC not perpendicular, construct OG perpendicular to CD and derive 'part greater than whole' contradiction. Alternative reasoning: perpendicular is shortest distance from centre to line, and OC is evidently shortest. This is converse/companion to XVI/XIX.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XIX — Theorem (right angle from tangent to centre)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a line (AB) be a tangent to a circle, the line (AC) drawn at right angles to it from the point of contact passes through the centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: if centre not in AC, derive contradiction using perpendicular properties; corollary: locus of centres of circles touching same line at same point is perpendicular at that point. Observation: Propositions XVI–XIX are interrelated and any two imply the third by identity; they are limiting cases of earlier propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XX — Theorem (central angle double circumference angle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The angle (AOB) at the centre (O) of a circle is double the angle (ACB) at the circumference standing on the same arc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof splits cases by position of C and uses isosceles triangle properties and angle-sum manipulations; corollary: angle in a semicircle is right (angle in semicircle is right angle). Theorem foundational for many angle-chord-arc relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXI — Theorem (angles in same segment equal)
rubrics_metrics.description: The angles (ACB, ADB) in the same segment of a circle are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: central angles double circumference angles, so halves equal. Alternate demonstration avoids angles > two right angles by producing auxiliary point E. Corollaries: 1) Four concyclic points if two triangles on same base with equal vertical angles. 2) Locus result: given base and vertex angle, locus of vertex is a circle. Exercises include many extremal and locus problems and classical results (e.g., equilateral triangle has max perimeter among inscribed triangles).

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXII — Theorem (opposite angles of cyclic quadrilateral supplementary)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sum of the opposite angles of a quadrilateral (ABCD) inscribed in a circle is two right angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via equal-segment angle relations or central-angle doubling. Corollary: an inscribed parallelogram is a rectangle. Exercises: many cyclic quadrilateral consequences, properties of hexagons, concurrency of perpendiculars, Simson line, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXIII — Theorem (no two similar segments on same chord, same side)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two similar segments of circles which do not coincide cannot be constructed on the same chord (AB), and on the same side of that chord.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction using the definition of similar segments (equal angles subtending arcs). Short proposition used to avoid ambiguous constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXIV — Theorem (similar segments on equal chords equal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar segments of circles (AEB, CFD) on equal chords (AB, CD) are equal to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: equal chords are congruent so matching similar segments must coincide; explained also by congruence under superposition. Useful for comparing arcs/segments when chords are equal. Exercises follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXV — Problem (construct circle from given arc)
rubrics_metrics.description: An arc (ABC) of a circle being given, it is required to describe the whole circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: take three points A,B,C on arc, bisect chords AB and BC, erect perpendiculars at bisectors; their intersection F is centre. Proof uses perpendicular bisector-through-centre property. This is the standard three-point-circle construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXVI — Observation / Theorem (relationships among Propositions XXVI–XXIX)
rubrics_metrics.description: The four Propositions XXVI–XXIX are so like in their enunciations that students frequently substitute one for another; scheme: relations among given equalities (angles, arcs, chords) in equal circles—Proposition XXVII is converse of XXVI and XXIX of XXVIII, etc. In equal circles, equal angles at centres or circumferences stand upon equal arcs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstration uses triangle congruence and the doubling relation between central and inscribed angles; corollaries include: (1) if opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are equal one diagonal is a diameter; (2) parallel chords intercept equal arcs; (3) relations for intersecting chords and arcs (sums/differences); (4) perpendicular-intercepted arcs sum to semicircle. Observation stresses pattern recognition for students.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXVII — Theorem (equal arcs → equal central/circumference angles)
rubrics_metrics.description: In equal circles (ACB, DFE), angles at the centres (AOB, DHE), or at the circumferences (ACB, DFE), which stand on equal arcs (AB, DE), are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction and congruence; if central angles differed, parts equal to whole contradiction. Follows directly from previous doubling/halving relations. Used to link arcs and angles when circles are equal.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXVIII — Theorem (equal chords divide circumferences into equal arcs)
rubrics_metrics.description: In equal circles (ACB, DFE), equal chords (AB, DE) divide the circumferences into arcs which are equal each to each—that is, the lesser to the lesser, and the greater to the greater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: equal chords imply equal central angles hence equal arcs; consider diameter case separately. Corollaries: parallel chords intercept equal arcs; exercises on loci and sliding segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXIX — Theorem (equal arcs subtend equal chords)
rubrics_metrics.description: In equal circles (ACB, DFE), equal arcs (AGB, DCK) are subtended by equal chords.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: equal arcs give equal central angles and congruent isosceles triangles, hence equal chord lengths. Observation: these four Propositions are immediate by congruence or superposition in equal circles.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXX — Problem (bisect a given arc)
rubrics_metrics.description: To bisect a given arc ACB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: draw chord AB, bisect AB at D, erect DC at right angles to AB to meet arc at C; then C bisects arc. Proof uses congruent right triangles ADC and BDC. Exercises: numerous related constructions and equalities when arcs/chords and bisectors are involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXXI — Theorem (angles in/greater/less than semicircle)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a circle—(1) The angle in a semicircle is a right angle. (2) The angle in a segment greater than a semicircle is an acute angle. (3) The angle in a segment less than a semicircle is an obtuse angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: central-angle doubling and angle-sum in triangle arguments; corollaries: diagonals of inscribed parallelogram meet at centre; practical constructions (find centre via carpenter’s square); draw two tangents from outside point. Exercises explore further consequences and constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXXII — Theorem (angle between tangent and chord equals angle in alternate segment)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a line (EF) be a tangent to a circle, and from the point of contact (A) a chord (AC) be drawn cutting the circle, the angles made by this line with the tangent are respectively equal to the angles in the alternate segments of the circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstration begins on page: classic tangent-chord theorem—angle between tangent and chord equals angle in opposite arc. This theorem ties tangents and inscribed angles; used extensively in solving angle-chord-tangent problems. (Proof continues beyond chunk.)
